summary: A messenger from overseas must have seen both the writing and the signing of the get. If he saw only part, or if different messengers saw different parts, the mishnah tells when it is valid.

chunks.en: Someone who brings a get from overseas and says,
chunks.st: With regard to one who brings a bill of divorce from a country overseas and says:

chunks.he: בְּפָנַי נִכְתַּב אֲבָל לֹא בְּפָנַי נֶחְתָּם,
chunks.en: "It was written in front of me, but not signed in front of me,"
chunks.st: The bill of divorce was written in my presence but it was not signed in my presence;

chunks.he: בְּפָנַי נֶחְתָּם אֲבָל לֹא בְּפָנַי נִכְתָּב,
chunks.en: "It was signed in front of me, but not written in front of me,"
chunks.st: or if he said: It was signed in my presence but it was not written in my presence;

chunks.he: בְּפָנַי נִכְתַּב כֻּלּוֹ וּבְפָנַי נֶחְתַּם חֶצְיוֹ,
chunks.en: "All of it was written in front of me, and half was signed in front of me,"
chunks.st: or: All of it was written in my presence and half of it was signed in my presence,
chunks.stMore: i.e., he observed the signing of only one witness; or:

chunks.he: בְּפָנַי נִכְתַּב חֶצְיוֹ וּבְפָנַי נֶחְתַּם כֻּלּוֹ,
chunks.en: "Half was written in front of me, and all of it was signed in front of me,"
chunks.st: Half of it was written in my presence and all of it was signed in my presence,

chunks.en: it is not valid. If one says "It was written in front of me,"
chunks.st: in all these cases the document is invalid. If one agent bringing a bill of divorce says: It was written in my presence,

chunks.en: and another says "It was signed in front of me,"
chunks.st: and one other agent says: It was signed in my presence,

chunks.en: it is not valid. If two say "It was written in front of us,"
chunks.st: it is invalid. If two agents say: It was written in our presence,

chunks.en: and one says "It was signed in front of me,"
chunks.st: and one says: It was signed in my presence,

chunks.en: it is not valid. But Rabbi Yehuda says it is valid.
chunks.st: it is invalid. And Rabbi Yehuda deems the document valid.

chunks.en: If one says "It was written in front of me,"
chunks.st: If one agent says: It was written in my presence,

chunks.en: and two say "It was signed in front of us," it is valid.
chunks.st: and two agents say: It was signed in our presence, it is valid.

summary: A get must be written and signed on the same day, counting the day from nightfall. Rabbi Shimon says a get is valid even if it was not.

chunks.en: If it was written in the day and signed in the day,
chunks.st: If a bill of divorce was written during the day and signed on the same day;

chunks.en: or written at night and signed at night,
chunks.st: or if it was written at night and signed on that same night;

chunks.en: or written at night and signed the next day,
chunks.st: or if it was written at night and signed on the following day,

chunks.en: it is valid. But written in the day and signed that night,
chunks.explain: A new day starts at night, so these are different days.
chunks.st: then it is valid.
chunks.stMore: The new calendar day begins at night, so that in all of these cases the writing and the signing were performed on the same date. However, if it was written during the day and signed on that same night,

chunks.en: it is not valid. Rabbi Shimon says it is valid,
chunks.st: it is invalid, as the writing and the signing were not on the same calendar day. Rabbi Shimon deems the bill of divorce valid.
chunks.stMore: The mishna explains the ruling of Rabbi Shimon:

chunks.en: for Rabbi Shimon used to say,
chunks.st: As Rabbi Shimon would say:

chunks.he: כָּל הַגִּטִּין שֶׁנִּכְתְּבוּ בַיּוֹם וְנֶחְתְּמוּ בַלַּיְלָה,
chunks.en: all documents written in the day and signed at night
chunks.st: All documents that were written during the day and signed at night

chunks.en: are not valid, except for gittin of women.
chunks.explain: A get is not used to collect money, so the date does not matter as much.
chunks.st: are invalid
chunks.stMore: because the date recorded in the document is a day prior to the day the document takes effect, except for women’s bills of divorce. Since a bill of divorce is not used to collect money, it is of no concern if the date that appears on it is before the time when it was signed.

summary: A get may be written with any ink that lasts, on almost anything. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says not on something alive and not on food.

chunks.en: We may write a get with anything,
chunks.st: One may write a bill of divorce with any material that can be used for writing:

chunks.en: with ink, with paint,
chunks.st: With deyo, with paint [sam],

chunks.en: with red paint, and with tree gum,
chunks.st: with sikra, with komos,

chunks.he: וּבְקַנְקַנְתּוֹם, וּבְכָל דָּבָר שֶׁהוּא שֶׁל קְיָמָא.
chunks.en: and with copper ink, or with anything that lasts.
chunks.st: with kankantom or with anything that produces permanent writing.

chunks.en: We do not write with liquids,
chunks.st: However, one may not write with other liquids,

chunks.en: nor with fruit juice,
chunks.st: nor with fruit juice,

chunks.en: nor with anything that does not last.
chunks.st: nor with anything that does not produce permanent writing.

chunks.en: We may write a get on anything,
chunks.st: Similarly, with regard to the document itself, one may write on anything,

chunks.en: on an olive leaf,
chunks.st: even on an olive leaf,

chunks.en: or on the horn of a cow,
chunks.st: or on the horn of a cow.

chunks.en: and he gives her the cow.
chunks.st: And the latter is valid if he gives her the entire cow.

chunks.en: Or on the hand of a slave,
chunks.st: Likewise, one may write a bill of divorce on the hand of a slave,

chunks.en: and he gives her the slave.
chunks.st: and that is valid if he gives her the slave.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili disagrees and says:

chunks.en: we may not write on a thing
chunks.st: One may not write a bill of divorce on any

chunks.en: that has a living spirit in it,
chunks.st: living thing,

chunks.en: nor on food.
chunks.st: nor may it be written on food.

summary: A get may not be written on something attached to the ground. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira also says not on erased paper or unfinished leather, but the Sages allow it.

chunks.en: We do not write a get on something attached to the ground.
chunks.st: One may not write a bill of divorce on anything that is attached to the ground.

chunks.en: If he wrote it on something attached,
chunks.st: If one wrote it on something that was attached to the ground, and afterward he

chunks.en: then cut it off, signed it, and gave it to her,
chunks.st: detached it, signed it, and gave it to her,

chunks.en: it is valid. Rabbi Yehuda says it is not valid,
chunks.st: then it is valid. Rabbi Yehuda deems a bill of divorce invalid

chunks.en: unless it is written and signed on something already cut off.
chunks.st: unless its writing and its signing were performed when it was already detached.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says:

chunks.en: we may not write on paper
chunks.st: One may not write a bill of divorce

chunks.en: that was erased, nor on unfinished leather,
chunks.st: on erased paper or on unfinished leather [diftera],

chunks.en: because it can be faked.
chunks.st: because writing on these surfaces can be forged.

chunks.en: But the Sages say it is valid.
chunks.st: And the Rabbis deem valid a bill of divorce that was written on either of these items.

summary: Anyone may write a get, because the witnesses who sign it are what count. But some people may not be the messenger who brings it.

chunks.en: Anyone may write the get,
chunks.st: Anyone is qualified to write a bill of divorce,

chunks.en: even a cheresh,
chunks.explain: A cheresh cannot hear or speak.
chunks.st: even a deaf-mute,

words.note: A person who cannot hear or speak.

chunks.en: a shoteh, or a child.
chunks.st: an imbecile, or a minor.

words.note: A person whose mind does not work clearly.

chunks.en: A woman may write her own get,
chunks.st: Additionally, a woman may write her own bill of divorce
chunks.stMore: and give it to her husband so that he can present it to her.

chunks.en: and a man may write his own receipt,
chunks.explain: The receipt says the wife was paid the money from her kesubah.
chunks.st: And a man may write his own receipt,
chunks.stMore: which must be given to him by the woman to confirm that he has paid her the value of her marriage contract.

chunks.en: because a get becomes valid only through the witnesses who sign it.
chunks.st: This is because the ratification of a bill of divorce is only through its signatories,
chunks.stMore: and it is irrelevant who wrote it.

chunks.en: Anyone may bring the get,
chunks.st: Anyone is fit to serve as an agent to bring a bill of divorce to a woman

chunks.en: except a cheresh,
chunks.st: except for a deaf-mute,

chunks.en: a shoteh, a child, a blind person, or a non-Jew.
chunks.st: an imbecile, or a minor, or a blind person, or a gentile.

summary: A messenger must be able to understand both when he gets the get and when he hands it over. If he was not able at the start, he cannot bring it.

chunks.en: If a child received the get and then grew up,
chunks.st: If a minor received the bill of divorce and then reached the age of majority,

chunks.en: or a cheresh who then could hear,
chunks.st: or one received it when he was a deaf-mute and then became able to hear,

chunks.en: or a blind man who then could see,
chunks.st: or one received it when he was blind and then became able to see,

chunks.en: or a shoteh who then became clear-minded,
chunks.st: or one received it when he was an imbecile and then became halakhically competent,

chunks.en: or a non-Jew who then became a Jew,
chunks.st: or one received it when he was a gentile and then converted,

words.note: A ger is someone who became Jewish.

chunks.he: פָּסוּל. אֲבָל פִּקֵּחַ וְנִתְחָרֵשׁ וְחָזַר וְנִתְפַּקֵּחַ,
chunks.en: he is not fit. But one who could hear, then became a cheresh, then could hear again,
chunks.st: in all of these cases he is unfit to bring the bill of divorce. However, if one received it when he was able to hear, and then became a deaf-mute, and then again became able to hear;

chunks.en: or could see, became blind, and then could see again,
chunks.st: or if one received it when he was able to see, and then became blind, and then again became able to see;

chunks.en: or was clear-minded, became a shoteh, and then became clear-minded again,
chunks.st: or one received it when he was halakhically competent, and then became an imbecile, and then again became halakhically competent,

chunks.en: he is fit. This is the rule:
chunks.st: in all of these cases he is fit to bring the bill of divorce. This is the principle:

chunks.en: anyone who understands at the start and at the end is fit.
chunks.st: Anyone who is halakhically competent in the beginning and in the end is fit, even if there was time in the interim when he was unfit.

summary: Some women may not tell us that a woman's husband died, but they may bring her get, because the written get proves it. A woman may even bring her own get.
stIntro: There are instances in which a woman’s testimony that another woman’s husband has died is not deemed credible (Yevamot 117a). If there is a presumption that due to their familial relationship the two women hate each other, there is concern that the woman is testifying falsely in order to harm the other woman. By doing so, she can cause the other woman to remarry. If her original husband then proves to be living, she will be required to leave her second husband. This mishna teaches:

chunks.en: Even the women who are not believed
chunks.st: Even the women who are not deemed credible to

chunks.en: to say that her husband died,
chunks.st: testify on behalf of a woman and say: Her husband died,

chunks.en: are believed to bring her get:
chunks.st: and she is permitted to remarry, are deemed credible to bring her bill of divorce.

chunks.en: her mother-in-law, her mother-in-law's daughter, and her husband's other wife,
chunks.st: The relatives of the woman who are not deemed credible to testify that her husband has died are: Her mother-in-law; and her mother-in-law’s daughter; and her rival wife, i.e., another wife of her husband’s;

words.note: Long ago a man could have two wives, and each one is the other's tzarah.

chunks.en: and her brother-in-law's wife, and her husband's daughter.
chunks.st: and her yevama, i.e., her husband’s brother’s wife; and her husband’s daughter.

chunks.en: What is the difference between a get and death?
chunks.st: The mishna explains: What is the difference between a bill of divorce and death,
chunks.stMore: that certain women are deemed credible to testify about one but not the other?

chunks.en: That the writing proves it.
chunks.st: With regard to a bill of divorce, it is so that the writing proves
chunks.stMore: that the husband is divorcing his wife, and the testimony is needed only to supplement the bill of divorce.

chunks.en: The woman herself may bring her own get,
chunks.st: Similarly, the woman herself may bring her own bill of divorce,

chunks.en: as long as she says,
chunks.st: provided that she is required by the court to state in its presence:

chunks.en: "It was written in front of me, and it was signed in front of me."
chunks.st: It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence, as the Gemara will explain.
